summaryBullets: That the sun go along the seven heavenly circles, which are the appointment of one hundred and eighty-two thrones, that it go down on a short day, and again one hundred and eighty-two, that it go down on a big day, and he has two thrones on which he rests, revolving here and there above the thrones of the months, from the seventeenth day of the month Tsivan it goes down to the month Thevan, from the seventeenth of Thevan it goes up. (48:1).
And thus it goes close to the earth, then the earth is glad and makes grow its fruits, and when it goes away, then the earth is sad, and trees and all fruits have no florescence. (48:2).
All this he measured, with good measurement of hours, and fixed A measure by his wisdom, of the visible (physical) and the invisible (spiritual). (48:3).
From the invisible (spiritual) he made all things visible (physical), himself being invisible (spiritual). (48:4).

Thus I make known to you, my children, and distribute the books to your children, into all your generations, and amongst the nations who shall have the sense to fear God, let them receive them, and may they come to love them more than any food or earthly sweets, and read them and apply themselves to them. (48:5).
And those who understand not the Lord, who fear not God, who accept not, but reject, who do not receive the (books), a terrible judgment awaits these. (48:6).
Blessed is the man who shall bear their yoke and shall drag them along, for he shall be released on the day of the great judgment. (48:7).
crossRefs: Genesis 8:22: While the earth remains, seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night shall not cease.
Esther 8:9: The third month, that is the month Sivan, is named in dating a decree, the month this chapter calls Tsivan.
Esther 2:16: The tenth month, which is the month Tebeth, is named in dating a king's year, the month this chapter calls Thevan.
Psalm 74:16-17: The day is thine and the night also, thou hast prepared the light and the sun, set the borders of the earth, and made summer and winter.
1 Enoch 82:4-6: The other Enoch book states its own reckoning, that the year is completed in three hundred and sixty-four days.

translationNotes.note: The two runs add up. One hundred and eighty-two for the shortening days and one hundred and eighty-two for the lengthening gives three hundred and sixty-four, and the two thrones the sun rests on bring the total to three hundred and sixty-six. That is the reckoning this chapter works with.

Sivan is the third month, falling across May and June, and Esther 8:9 names it when dating a decree. The chapter puts the sun's turn on the seventeenth of it, which lands close to the longest day of the year.

Tebeth is the tenth month, falling across December and January, and Esther 2:16 names it. The chapter has the sun begin to climb on the seventeenth of it, close to the shortest day, so the two dates mark the two turning points.

translationNotes.term: Two thrones on which he rests
translationNotes.note: The resting points are the solstices, the days at each end of the year when the sun stops shifting along the horizon and turns back the other way. The Latin word solstice says exactly that: the sun standing still.

translationNotes.term: The earth is glad and makes grow its fruits
translationNotes.note: The growing season in that region depends on the sun's height and the winter rains together. Deuteronomy 11:14 pairs the early and the latter rain with corn, wine and oil, and Deuteronomy 33:14 speaks of the precious fruits brought forth by the sun.

translationNotes.term: Bear their yoke and drag them along
translationNotes.note: The books are described as a load to be hauled, not as a comfort. The image is a working animal under a yoke, and the blessing falls on the man who takes the weight, which is how the chapter answers the judgment threatened on those who refuse them.

stories.keyTakeaway: The sun runs one hundred and eighty-two thrones down and the same number up, with two resting thrones at the turns, descending from the seventeenth of Tsivan and climbing from the seventeenth of Thevan. Enoch tells his sons to pass the books to every nation that will fear God.

stories.title: 📜 2 Enoch (Secrets of Enoch) 49
summaryBullets: I swear to you, my children, but I swear not by any oath, neither by heaven nor by earth, nor by any other creature which God created. (49:1).
The Lord said: There is no oath in me, nor injustice, but truth. (49:2).
If there is no truth in men, let them swear by the words, Yea, yea, or else, Nay, nay. (49:3).

And I swear to you, yea, yea, that there has been no man in his mother's womb, (but that) already before, even to each one there is a place prepared for the repose of that soul, and a measure fixed how much it is intended that a man be tried in this world. (49:4).
Yea, children, deceive not yourselves, for there has been previously prepared a place for every soul of man. (49:5).
crossRefs: Matthew 5:33-37: Swear not at all, neither by heaven nor by the earth nor by thy head, but let your communication be Yea, yea, Nay, nay.
James 5:12: Above all things swear not, neither by heaven nor by earth, but let your yea be yea and your nay be nay, lest ye fall into condemnation.
Psalm 139:15-16: My substance was not hid from thee when I was made in secret, and in thy book all my members were written before there were any of them.
2 Esdras 7:32: The earth shall restore those that sleep in her, and the secret places shall deliver up the souls committed to them.
Deuteronomy 6:13: Thou shalt fear the LORD thy God and serve him and shalt swear by his name, so the law commands an oath in the name.

translationNotes.term: I swear not by any oath
translationNotes.note: Enoch refuses to swear by anything created. Deuteronomy 6:13 commands swearing by the name of the LORD, and Matthew 5:34-36 forbids swearing by heaven, earth or Jerusalem because every one of them belongs to God. This chapter refuses that same list.

translationNotes.term: Yea, yea, or else, Nay, nay
translationNotes.original: Greek: ναὶ ναί, οὒ οὔ (nai nai, ou ou)
translationNotes.note: The doubled word is a plain answer with nothing added to prop it up. Matthew 5:37 gives the identical formula and James 5:12 repeats it, saying let your yea be yea and your nay be nay.

translationNotes.term: A measure fixed how much a man be tried
translationNotes.note: Each life is said to arrive with a set quantity of testing already assigned to it, not only a resting place. The book states it as an amount weighed out in advance, which is why the next line warns the hearers not to deceive themselves about it.

translationNotes.term: A place prepared for the repose of that soul
translationNotes.note: The book has chambers of rest prepared for souls before birth. 2 Esdras 7:32 speaks of secret places delivering up the souls committed to them, and 1 Enoch 22:1-4 shows Enoch four hollow places where the spirits of the dead are held until judgment.

translationNotes.term: There is no oath in me
translationNotes.note: The reason given for not swearing is that God has no need of it. An oath calls a higher witness, and there is none above him. Hebrews 6:13 states that outright, that when God made promise to Abraham he could swear by no greater, so he swore by himself.

stories.keyTakeaway: Enoch swears without an oath, refusing heaven, earth and every creature, and tells his sons to answer yes or no plainly instead. He then says every soul has a place prepared before birth and a fixed measure of testing set for it.

stories.title: 📜 2 Enoch (Secrets of Enoch) 50
summaryBullets: I have put every man's work in writing and none born on earth can remain hidden nor his works remain concealed. (50:1).
I see all things. (50:2).
Now therefore, my children, in patience and meekness spend the number of your days, that you inherit endless life. (50:3).
Endure for the sake of the Lord every wound, every injury, every evil word and attack. (50:4).

If ill-requitals befall you, return (them) not either to neighbour or enemy, because the Lord will return (them) for you and be your avenger on the day of great judgment, that there be no avenging here among men. (50:5).
Whoever of you spends gold or silver for his brother's sake, he will receive ample treasure in the world to come. (50:6).
Injure not widows nor orphans nor strangers, lest God's wrath come upon you. (50:7).
crossRefs: Leviticus 19:18: Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge against the children of thy people, but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.
Deuteronomy 32:35: To me belongeth vengeance and recompence, so the settling of accounts is reserved to God and not left to the injured man.
Romans 12:19: Avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath, for it is written, Vengeance is mine, I will repay, saith the Lord.
Exodus 22:21-24: Ye shall not vex a stranger nor afflict any widow or fatherless child, and if they cry at all unto me I will surely hear their cry.
Matthew 6:19-20: Lay not up treasure on earth where moth and rust corrupt, but lay up treasure in heaven where thieves do not break through nor steal.

translationNotes.term: That there be no avenging here among men
translationNotes.note: Private retaliation is ruled out, not justice itself. Leviticus 19:18 forbids taking vengeance and bearing a grudge, and Deuteronomy 32:35 reserves vengeance to God, the verse Paul quotes when he tells believers never to avenge themselves.

The word does not mean weakness. In Greek it was used of a horse broken to the bridle, strength that answers the rein. Numbers 12:3 calls Moses the meekest man on the face of the earth in the middle of an account of him governing a nation.

A ger is a resident foreigner living among Israel with no land and no clan to protect him. Exodus 23:9 gives the reason for the law that shields him, that Israel knew the heart of a stranger in Egypt, and Leviticus 19:34 orders that he be loved as oneself.

A requital is a repayment, so ill-requitals are injuries paid back in kind. The instruction here is that the chain stops with the man who took the first blow, and it makes no distinction between a neighbour and an enemy.

Days are counted rather than open-ended. Psalm 90:12 asks God to teach us to number our days that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom, and this line uses that same reckoning as the reason for patience.

stories.keyTakeaway: Enoch tells his sons to take injury without paying it back, because the Lord will settle the account and there is to be no vengeance among men. Money spent on a brother earns treasure later, and widows, orphans and strangers are not to be harmed.

stories.title: 📜 2 Enoch (Secrets of Enoch) 51
summaryBullets: Stretch out your hands to the poor according to your strength. (51:1).
Hide not your silver in the earth. (51:2).
Help the faithful man in affliction, and affliction will not find you in the time of your trouble. (51:3).
And every grievous and cruel yoke that come upon you bear all for the sake of the Lord, and thus you will find your reward in the day of judgment. (51:4).
It is good to go morning, midday, and evening into the Lord's dwelling, for the glory of your creator. (51:5).
Because every breathing (thing) glorifies him, and every creature visible (physical) and invisible (spiritual) returns him praise. (51:6).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 15:7-11: Thou shalt not shut thine hand from thy poor brother but open thine hand wide unto him, for the poor shall never cease out of the land.
Proverbs 19:17: He that hath pity upon the poor lendeth unto the LORD, and that which he hath given will he pay him again.
Matthew 25:18: The servant who received one talent went and digged in the earth and hid his lord's money there.
Psalm 55:17: Evening and morning and at noon will I pray and cry aloud, and he shall hear my voice.
Daniel 6:10: Daniel kneeled upon his knees three times a day, prayed and gave thanks before his God as he had always done.

translationNotes.term: Hide not your silver in the earth
translationNotes.note: Burying money was the ordinary way of securing it where there were no banks and no locks worth trusting. Matthew 25:18 has a servant do exactly that, and Matthew 25:25 has him admit he hid the talent in the ground because he was afraid, so the practice is assumed and then judged.

Three times a day is the fixed pattern. Psalm 55:17 names evening, morning and noon, Daniel 6:10 has a man kneel three times a day at open windows, and Acts 3:1 shows the rhythm still running, with the ninth hour called the hour of prayer.

Mishkan means a dwelling place and it is the word for the tabernacle, the tent God is said to dwell in among the people at Exodus 25:8. This chapter uses it of somewhere a man walks to three times a day, not of heaven.

Giving is measured against what a man actually has. Tobit 4:8 states the same rule, that if you have abundance give alms accordingly, and if you have little, do not be afraid to give according to that little.

The yoke image runs both ways in this book. Here the load is to be carried for the Lord's sake, while earlier the same word covers God's own yoke that the generations threw off. Either way the picture is a working animal in harness.

stories.keyTakeaway: Enoch tells his sons to give to the poor as far as their strength goes, not to bury their silver, to help the faithful in trouble and to carry every hard yoke for the Lord, and to go into the Lord's dwelling morning, midday and evening.

stories.title: 📜 2 Enoch (Secrets of Enoch) 52
summaryBullets: Blessed is the man who opens his lips in praise of God of Sabaoth and praises the Lord with his heart. (52:1).
Cursed every man who opens his lips for the bringing into contempt and calumny of his neighbour, because he brings God into contempt. (52:2).
Blessed is he who opens his lips blessing and praising God. (52:3).
Cursed is he before the Lord all the days of his life, who opens his lips to curse and abuse. (52:4).
Blessed is he who blesses all the Lord's works. (52:5).
Cursed is he who brings the Lord's creation into contempt. (52:6).
Blessed is he who looks down and raises the fallen. (52:7).
Cursed is he who looks to and is eager for the destruction of what is not his. (52:8).
Blessed is he who keeps the foundations of his fathers made firm from the beginning. (52:9).
Cursed is he who perverts the decrees of his forefathers. (52:10).
Blessed is he who imparts peace and love. (52:11).
Cursed is he who disturbs those that love their neighbours. (52:12).
Blessed is he who speaks with humble tongue and heart to all. (52:13).
Cursed is he who speaks peace with his tongue, while in his heart there is no peace but a sword. (52:14).
For all these things will be laid bare in the weighing-scales and in the books, on the day of the great judgment. (52:15).
crossRefs: Deuteronomy 27:15-26: The Levites pronounce a run of curses over the people and all the people answer Amen to every one of them.
Deuteronomy 11:29: The blessing is to be set on Mount Gerizim and the curse on Mount Ebal when Israel comes into the land.
Psalm 1:1-6: The way of the righteous is set against the way of the ungodly, the same two-column arrangement this chapter uses.
Matthew 5:3-12: A run of blessings pronounced one after another, each naming who is blessed and what follows for them.
Psalm 55:21: The words of his mouth were smoother than butter but war was in his heart, softer than oil yet they were drawn swords.

translationNotes.note: The two words open a formal pronouncement, not a wish. Deuteronomy 27:15-26 has the Levites call out a series of curses with the people answering Amen to each, and Deuteronomy 11:29 puts the blessing on Gerizim and the curse on Ebal, the two hills that flank Shechem.

Keeping the foundations means leaving an inherited boundary where it was set. Proverbs 22:28 says remove not the ancient landmark which thy fathers have set, and Deuteronomy 19:14 forbids moving a neighbour's landmark, a boundary stone that could be shifted at night with nobody the wiser.

Calumny is slander, a false charge made to do damage. The Greek word for a slanderer is diabolos, from a verb meaning to throw across or to accuse, and it is the word English turns into devil. Exodus 23:1 forbids raising a false report outright.

translationNotes.term: Peace with his tongue, a sword in his heart
translationNotes.note: Psalm 55:21 says the same thing in the same shape, words smoother than butter with war in the heart. Jeremiah 9:8 calls the tongue an arrow shot out, speaking peaceably to a neighbour while laying wait for him inside.

Two instruments of record named together, a balance and a ledger. Daniel 5:27 has a man weighed in the balances and found wanting, and Revelation 20:12 has the dead judged out of the things written in the books.

Lifting up someone who has gone down is a physical picture, and it was already one of the marks of the righteous listed at the third heaven earlier in this book. Psalm 145:14 says the LORD upholdeth all that fall and raiseth up all those that be bowed down.

stories.keyTakeaway: Enoch runs a list of blessings and curses in pairs: the tongue that praises against the tongue that slanders, the hand that lifts a fallen man against the hand that reaches for what is not his, and peace spoken with a sword behind it. He closes with the scales and the books.

stories.title: 📜 2 Enoch (Secrets of Enoch) 53
summaryBullets: And now, my children, do not say: Our father is standing before God, and is praying for our sins, for there is there no helper of any man who has sinned. (53:1).

You see how I wrote all works of every man, before his creation, (all) that is done amongst all men for all time, and none can tell or relate my handwriting, because the Lord see all imaginings of man, how they are vain, where they lie in the treasure-houses of the heart. (53:2).
And now, my children, mark well all the words of your father, that I tell you, lest you regret, saying: Why did our father not tell us? (53:3).
crossRefs: Ezekiel 14:14: Though Noah, Daniel and Job were in it, they should deliver but their own souls by their righteousness.
Ezekiel 18:20: The soul that sinneth, it shall die, and the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father nor the father the iniquity of the son.
Jeremiah 15:1: Though Moses and Samuel stood before me, yet my mind could not be toward this people.
Psalm 49:7-8: None of them can by any means redeem his brother nor give to God a ransom for him, for the redemption of their soul is costly.
Jeremiah 17:9-10: The heart is deceitful above all things and desperately wicked, and the LORD searches the heart and tries the reins.

translationNotes.term: Our father is standing before God
translationNotes.note: The objection being ruled out is that a famous ancestor will cover for his descendants. Matthew 3:9 rules out the same argument in different words, warning men not to think it enough to say they have Abraham for their father.

translationNotes.term: No helper of any man who has sinned
translationNotes.note: Scripture states the same limit. Ezekiel 14:14 says that even Noah, Daniel and Job would deliver only their own souls, and Ezekiel 18:20 says the son does not carry the father's iniquity. This book puts the rule in the mouth of the father who is about to be prayed to.

The storeroom word this book used for the snow, the dew and the winds is turned on a man's inner life, so thoughts become stock held under lock and key. Matthew 12:35 uses the same image of a good man bringing forth good things out of the good treasure of the heart.

Yetser means what is shaped or formed, from the verb used of a potter working clay. Genesis 6:5 says every imagination of the thoughts of man's heart was only evil continually, and Genesis 8:21 repeats it after the flood.

translationNotes.term: Why did our father not tell us
translationNotes.note: Naming the excuse in advance puts the responsibility on the hearers. Ezekiel 3:17-19 works the same way from the other side, where a watchman who fails to warn carries the blood and one who warns is clear of it.

stories.keyTakeaway: Enoch forbids his sons to count on him praying for them once he is gone, saying there is no helper there for a man who has sinned, and tells them to take his words now so that they never ask why they were not told.

stories.title: 📜 2 Enoch (Secrets of Enoch) 54
summaryBullets: At that time, not understanding this let these books which I have given you be for an inheritance of your peace. (54:1).
Hand them to all who want them, and instruct them, that they may see the Lord's very great and marvellous works. (54:2).
crossRefs: Proverbs 13:22: A good man leaveth an inheritance to his children's children, so what is handed down is counted as property.
Deuteronomy 6:6-9: These words shall be in thine heart, and thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children and talk of them at home and on the road.
Deuteronomy 31:12-13: Gather the people, men, women, children and the stranger within thy gates, that they may hear and learn and fear the LORD.
Psalm 145:4: One generation shall praise thy works to another and shall declare thy mighty acts.
Isaiah 38:19: The father to the children shall make known thy truth, the living, the living, he shall praise thee.

translationNotes.note: An inheritance is normally land. Calling the books an inheritance of peace makes the text itself the family holding, and shalom means wholeness and safety rather than only the absence of fighting.

translationNotes.term: Hand them to all who want them
translationNotes.note: The distribution is open and not restricted to the family. That is the reverse of Daniel 12:4, where the words are shut up and the book sealed until the time of the end, and it matches this book's repeated order to spread copies among the nations.

Handing over a text is not treated as enough by itself, and teaching goes with it. Nehemiah 8:8 shows what that meant in practice, reading the book distinctly and giving the sense so that the people understood what was read.

Niflaot means wonders, acts beyond what men can do, and Psalm 145:5 uses it of God's wondrous works. In this book the wonders are the workings of the heavens and the weather that Enoch was shown, not signs done among people.

stories.keyTakeaway: Enoch leaves the books as the inheritance of his sons' peace and tells them to hand them to anyone who wants them and to teach from them, so that others can see what the Lord has made and done.

stories.title: 📜 2 Enoch (Secrets of Enoch) 55
summaryBullets: My children, behold, the day of my term and time have approached. (55:1).
For the angels who shall go with me are standing before me and urge me to my departure from you; they are standing here on earth, awaiting what has been told them. (55:2).
For to-morrow I shall go up on to heaven, to the uppermost Jerusalem to my eternal inheritance. (55:3).
Therefore I bid you do before the Lord's face all (his) good pleasure. (55:4).
crossRefs: Galatians 4:26: Jerusalem which is above is free, which is the mother of us all.
Hebrews 12:22: Ye are come unto the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to an innumerable company of angels.
Revelation 21:2: The holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.
2 Kings 2:9-11: Elijah knows the day he is to be taken, and a chariot of fire parts him from Elisha as he goes up by a whirlwind into heaven.
2 Timothy 4:6-8: Paul says the time of his departure is at hand and that a crown is laid up for him, the same shape of a stated last day.

translationNotes.original: Greek: ἡ ἄνω Ἰερουσαλήμ (he ano Ierousalem)
translationNotes.note: A heavenly city answering to the earthly one. Galatians 4:26 calls it Jerusalem which is above, Hebrews 12:22 the heavenly Jerusalem, and Revelation 21:2 the new Jerusalem coming down out of heaven. This book compresses the idea into a single phrase.

The thirty days granted earlier have run out, so this is a schedule closing rather than a premonition. The book keeps the count in view all the way through and gives the exact date of the departure in its final chapter.

translationNotes.term: They are standing here on earth
translationNotes.note: The two guides who brought him down were told to wait for the determined day, and this line reports them still standing there thirty days later. The book keeps track of its own characters across chapters instead of dropping them.

An everlasting holding. In the law a nachalah is family land that cannot be sold away for good, and Numbers 18:20 says the LORD himself is the portion and the inheritance of the priests, who are given no land at all.

Ratson means will, favour, or what pleases, and it works both for a man being accepted and for what God wants done. Psalm 143:10 asks to be taught to do God's will using that word, which is what Enoch is telling them to do here.

stories.keyTakeaway: Enoch says his time is up, that the angels who will take him are already standing on the earth waiting, and that tomorrow he goes up to the uppermost Jerusalem, which he calls his eternal inheritance.

stories.title: 📜 2 Enoch (Secrets of Enoch) 56
summaryBullets: Mathosalam (Methuselah) having answered his father Enoch, said: What is agreeable to your eyes, father, that I may make before your face, that you may bless our dwellings, and your sons, and that your people may be made glorious through you, and then (that) you may depart thus, as the Lord said? (56:1).

Enoch answered to his son Mathosalam (Methuselah) (and) said: Hear, child, from the time when the Lord anointed me with the ointment of his glory, (there has been no) food in me, and my soul remembers not earthly enjoyment, neither do I want anything earthly. (56:2).
crossRefs: Judges 13:15-16: Manoah presses the angel to stay while he makes ready a kid, and the angel answers that though he stays he will not eat of his bread.
Tobit 12:19: All these days I did appear unto you, but I did neither eat nor drink, but ye did see a vision.
Genesis 18:6-8: Abraham has a calf dressed with cakes, butter and milk and sets it before his three visitors under the tree, and they eat.
Exodus 34:28: Moses was there with the LORD forty days and forty nights and did neither eat bread nor drink water.
Matthew 4:4: Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God.

translationNotes.term: That you may bless our dwellings
translationNotes.note: A father's blessing before he died was a formal act with legal weight, not a farewell wish. Genesis 27:1-4 has Isaac ask for a meal first and then bless, which is the sequence Methuselah is trying to set up here.

translationNotes.term: There has been no food in me
translationNotes.note: The anointing is given as the reason he no longer eats, so the change is presented as physical and permanent. Judges 13:16 has an angel refuse Manoah's food outright, and Tobit 12:19 has one explain afterwards that what the family saw was appearance only.

The same anointing described at the throne, where Michael took Enoch out of his earthly garments, anointed him and dressed him in the garments of glory. This chapter reports what that did to him once he was back on earth.

translationNotes.term: My soul remembers not earthly enjoyment
translationNotes.note: Nefesh means the whole living self and it can mean appetite outright; Proverbs 27:7 says the full soul loathes a honeycomb. Saying his soul does not remember earthly enjoyment is a statement about hunger as much as about memory.

The same son called Mathusal in the opening chapter, spelled differently here. Slavonic copies vary in how they render the Greek forms of Hebrew names, and this book carries more than one spelling for the same man.

stories.keyTakeaway: Methuselah asks to prepare something so his father can bless the household before he goes. Enoch answers that since the Lord anointed him with the ointment of his glory there has been no food in him and he wants nothing on earth at all.

stories.title: 📜 2 Enoch (Secrets of Enoch) 57
summaryBullets: My child Methosalam (Methuselah), summon all your brethren and all your household and the elders of the people, that I may talk to them and depart, as is planned for me. (57:1).

And Methosalam (Methuselah) made haste, and summoned his brethren, Regim, Riman, Uchan, Chermion, Gaidad, and all the elders of the people before the face of his father Enoch; and he blessed them, (and) said to them: (57:2).
crossRefs: Genesis 5:22: Enoch walked with God after he begat Methuselah, and begat sons and daughters, none of whom are named there.
Genesis 48:8-16: Jacob blesses Joseph's sons before he dies, laying his hands on their heads and naming the God who fed him all his life long.
Deuteronomy 33:1: This is the blessing wherewith Moses the man of God blessed the children of Israel before his death.
Exodus 24:1: Moses is told to come up with Aaron, Nadab, Abihu and seventy of the elders of Israel, who worship afar off.
Numbers 11:16-17: Seventy men of the elders of the people are gathered to stand with Moses and bear the burden of the people with him.

translationNotes.note: Five sons of Enoch besides Methuselah, named only in this book. Genesis 5:22 says Enoch fathered sons and daughters and gives none of their names. Two of these, Regim and Gaidad, were already named in the opening chapter.

Elders were the heads of families who sat at the gate, judged cases and spoke for the community. Exodus 24:1 and Numbers 11:16 both treat them as a standing body, so summoning them turns a family gathering into a public assembly.

A blessing here is a formal act done before witnesses, usually with hands laid on, as Genesis 48:14 describes Jacob doing over Joseph's sons. It transferred standing, and once given it was not taken back.

translationNotes.term: That I may talk to them and depart
translationNotes.note: The order of these closing chapters is fixed: summon, speak, bless, then go. Deuteronomy 33:1 gives the same sequence for Moses, a blessing on the tribes immediately before his death, and this book follows it.

stories.keyTakeaway: Enoch has Methuselah summon his brothers and the elders of the people so he can speak to them all before he leaves, and the brothers are named: Regim, Riman, Uchan, Chermion and Gaidad.

stories.title: 📜 2 Enoch (Secrets of Enoch) 58
summaryBullets: Listen to me, my children, to-day. (58:1).

In those days when the Lord came down on to earth for Adam's sake, and visited all his creatures, which he created himself, after all these he created Adam, and the Lord called all the beasts of the earth, all the reptiles, and all the birds that soar in the air, and brought them all before the face of our father Adam. (58:2).
And Adam gave the names to all things living on earth. (58:3).

And the Lord appointed him ruler over all, and subjected to him all things under his hands, and made them dumb and made them dull that they be commanded of man, and be in subjection and obedience to him. (58:4).
Thus also the Lord created every man lord over all his possessions. (58:5).
The Lord will not judge a single soul of beast for man's sake, but adjudges the souls of men to their beasts in this world; for men have a special place. (58:6).

And as every soul of man is according to number, similarly beasts will not perish, nor all souls of beasts which the Lord created, till the great judgment, and they will accuse man, if he feed them ill. (58:7).
crossRefs: Genesis 2:19-20: God brings every beast and every fowl to Adam to see what he would call them, and whatever Adam called each one was its name.
Genesis 1:28: God blesses them and gives them dominion over the fish, the fowl and every living thing that moves upon the earth.
Proverbs 12:10: A righteous man regardeth the life of his beast, but the tender mercies of the wicked are cruel.
Exodus 20:10: The sabbath rest covers the cattle along with the household, the servants and the stranger inside the gates.
Deuteronomy 25:4: Thou shalt not muzzle the ox when he treadeth out the corn, so the animal doing the work eats while it works.

translationNotes.note: Naming is an act of authority in this world, not the handing out of labels. Genesis 2:19 has God bring the animals to see what the man would call them, and Genesis 17:5 and Genesis 32:28 both show a change of name marking a change of standing.

translationNotes.term: They will accuse man, if he feed them ill
translationNotes.note: The book has animals bring a charge at the judgment. Scripture requires that a working animal be fed and rested, at Deuteronomy 25:4 and Exodus 20:10, and Proverbs 12:10 makes care for a beast a mark of a righteous man. Animals appearing as accusers is this book's own claim.

The Hebrew phrase living soul is used of the animals at Genesis 1:20-21 and Genesis 1:24 before it is used of the man at Genesis 2:7. English hides that by rendering the same two words living creature for the animals and living soul for the man.

translationNotes.term: Made them dumb and made them dull
translationNotes.note: The book explains animal silence as something done to them at the naming so that they could be commanded. Genesis records no such act. This is the book's own explanation for a state of affairs any reader can see for himself.

The chapter keeps a line between men and beasts while giving both a soul that survives. Ecclesiastes 3:19-21 sets the two side by side and asks who knows whether the spirit of one goes upward and the other goes downward, and Psalm 8:5-8 puts man under God and over the works of his hands.

stories.keyTakeaway: Enoch recalls Adam naming the animals and being set over them as ruler, and then says the beasts have souls that last until the great judgment, where they will bring a charge against any man who fed them badly.

stories.title: 📜 2 Enoch (Secrets of Enoch) 59
summaryBullets: Whoever defiles the soul of beasts, defiles his own soul. (59:1).
For man brings clean animals to make sacrifice for sin, that he may have cure of his soul. (59:2).
And if they bring for sacrifice clean animals, and birds, man has cure, he cures his soul. (59:3).
All is given you for food, bind it by the four feet, that is to make good the cure, he cures his soul. (59:4).
But whoever kills beast without wounds, kills his own souls and defiles his own flesh. (59:5).
And he who does any beast any injury whatever, in secret, it is evil practice, and he defiles his own soul. (59:6).
crossRefs: Leviticus 1:3-9: The burnt offering is brought to the door, the man lays his hand on its head, it is killed, and the priests handle the blood and the pieces.
Leviticus 11:1-8: Clean and unclean beasts are separated by two physical tests, chewing the cud and dividing the hoof, and the unclean are not to be eaten.
Genesis 7:2: Noah is told to take clean beasts by sevens and unclean by twos, so the distinction is already in force long before Sinai.
Psalm 118:27: Bind the sacrifice with cords, even unto the horns of the altar.
Genesis 9:3-4: Every moving thing is given for food, but flesh with the life in it, which is the blood, is not to be eaten.

translationNotes.note: Clean does not mean washed. Leviticus 11:1-8 fixes it for land animals by two physical tests, chewing the cud and a divided hoof, and Genesis 7:2 already has Noah sorting clean from unclean long before that law was written down.

translationNotes.term: Bind it by the four feet
translationNotes.note: An animal for sacrifice was tied so that it could be handled and killed cleanly. Psalm 118:27 says bind the sacrifice with cords to the horns of the altar, and Genesis 22:9 uses the same verb of Isaac being bound and laid on the wood.

The phrase describes a kill that is not a clean cut, so strangling or beating rather than a knife across the throat. Acts 15:20 keeps things strangled on a short list of what to abstain from, and Genesis 9:4 forbids eating flesh with the blood still in it.

The verb behind atonement means to cover over or wipe clean, and Leviticus 17:11 says the blood makes atonement for the soul. The translation here says cure, which keeps the sense of something healed rather than merely excused.

Cruelty done where nobody can see is named as its own case. Deuteronomy 27:15-24 does the same thing repeatedly, cursing the man who acts in secret, because the whole point of that list is conduct no court will ever hear about.

stories.keyTakeaway: Enoch says a man who abuses an animal defiles himself. Clean beasts and birds brought as sacrifice heal a man's soul, killing without a proper cut does the reverse, and injuring a beast in secret still counts against him.

stories.title: 📜 2 Enoch (Secrets of Enoch) 60
summaryBullets: He who works the killing of a man's soul, kills his own soul, and kills his own body, and there is no cure for him for all time. (60:1).
He who puts a man in any snare, shall stick in it himself, and there is no cure for him for all time. (60:2).
He who puts a man in any vessel, his retribution will not be wanting at the great judgment for all time. (60:3).
He who works crookedly or speaks evil against any soul, will not make justice for himself for all time. (60:4).
crossRefs: Numbers 35:30-31: No man is put to death on the word of one witness, and no ransom may be taken for the life of a murderer who is guilty of death.
Psalm 7:15-16: He made a pit and digged it and is fallen into the ditch he made, and his violent dealing comes down upon his own head.
Proverbs 26:27: Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein, and he that rolleth a stone, it will return upon him.
Esther 7:9-10: Haman is hanged on the gallows he had made ready for Mordecai, fifty cubits high and standing at his own house.
Exodus 20:13: Thou shalt not kill, the sixth commandment, which in Hebrew bans unlawful killing rather than all killing.

translationNotes.note: The verb in the sixth commandment at Exodus 20:13 is ratsach, unlawful killing, which is why murder is the right rendering and kill is too wide, since the same law hands down capital sentences and sends armies out. It is not simply murder either: Numbers 35:11 uses the same root of a man who kills unintentionally and sends him to a city of refuge.

translationNotes.term: No cure for him for all time
translationNotes.note: A kofer is a payment made in place of a penalty. Numbers 35:31 forbids taking one for the life of a murderer, so a killing cannot be settled with money, and Numbers 35:30 requires more than one witness before anyone is put to death at all.

translationNotes.term: Puts a man in any snare
translationNotes.note: A snare is a hunting trap, a noose or a spring-set net laid on a path for birds and small game. Psalm 7:15-16 and Proverbs 26:27 both turn the trap back on the man who set it, and Esther 7:10 shows it happening to a man by name.

translationNotes.term: Puts a man in any vessel
translationNotes.note: The phrase is obscure and the translation keeps it literal rather than smoothing it into something readable. It sits in a list of ways of getting hold of a person, between setting a snare and dealing crookedly, and the text offers no explanation.

translationNotes.term: Will not make justice for himself
translationNotes.note: The picture is a court case a man cannot win. The wording puts him at the great judgment arguing his own defence with nothing to say, which is why the chapters around it keep pointing at the books and the scales.

stories.keyTakeaway: Enoch turns to what a man does to a man: killing destroys the killer with no remedy left, a trap set catches the one who set it, and crooked dealing or evil speech leaves a man with no case at the great judgment.

stories.title: 📜 2 Enoch (Secrets of Enoch) 61
summaryBullets: And now, my children, keep your hearts from every injustice, which the Lord hates. Just as a man asks something for his own soul from God, so let him do to every living soul, because I know all things, how in the great time to come there is much inheritance prepared for men, good for the good, and bad for the bad, without number many. (61:1).
Blessed are those who enter the good houses, for in the bad houses there is no peace nor return from them. (61:2).

Hear, my children, small and great! When man puts a good thought in his heart, brings gifts from his labours before the Lord's face and his hands made them not, then the Lord will turn away his face from the labour of his hand, and (that) man cannot find the labour of his hands. (61:3).
And if his hands made it, but his heart murmur, and his heart cease not making murmur incessantly, he has not any advantage. (61:4).
crossRefs: Matthew 7:12: Whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them, for this is the law and the prophets.
Tobit 4:15: Do that to no man which thou hatest, the same rule stated from the other side.
John 14:2: In my Father's house are many mansions, and I go to prepare a place for you.
2 Corinthians 9:7: Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give, not grudgingly nor of necessity, for God loveth a cheerful giver.
Deuteronomy 15:10: Thou shalt surely give him, and thine heart shall not be grieved when thou givest unto him, and the LORD shall bless thee.

translationNotes.term: So let him do to every living soul
translationNotes.note: The rule is set as a measure a man takes off himself first. Matthew 7:12 puts it positively, do to others what you would have done to you, and Tobit 4:15 puts it negatively, do to no man what you hate. This chapter widens it to every living soul, which in this book takes in animals.

translationNotes.term: The good houses and the bad houses
translationNotes.note: The Greek word for a dwelling of this kind means a lodging or resting place. John 14:2 says in my Father's house are many mansions, using that word, and mansions in older English simply means places to stay. This chapter has two sets of them, and from the bad ones there is no way back.

A gift has to come out of the giver's own work. Deuteronomy 26:1-11 has the firstfruits carried in a basket with a spoken declaration of where the produce came from, so an offering was tied to a particular field and a particular harvest.

Murmuring has a fixed sense in this vocabulary. Exodus 16:2-8 uses it of the whole camp complaining in the wilderness and Numbers 14:27 has God answer the murmurings directly. It means grumbling that keeps going, not a single complaint.

The reward is described as an estate already made ready and standing empty rather than a wage paid at the end. This book said the same about the places prepared for souls before birth, so both ends of a life are described as furnished in advance.

stories.keyTakeaway: Enoch gives the rule of doing to every living soul what a man asks for his own, describes the good houses and the bad houses prepared for men, and says a gift made by other hands or brought with a grumbling heart earns nothing.

stories.title: 📜 2 Enoch (Secrets of Enoch) 62
summaryBullets: Blessed is the man who in his patience brings his gifts with faith before the Lord's face, because he will find forgiveness of sins. (62:1).
But if he take back his words before the time, there is no repentance for him; and if the time pass and he do not of his own will what is promised, there is no repentance after death. (62:2).
Because every work which man does before the time, is all deceit before men, and sin before God. (62:3).
crossRefs: Ecclesiastes 5:4-5: When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it, for better is it that thou shouldest not vow than that thou shouldest vow and not pay.
Deuteronomy 23:21-23: When thou shalt vow a vow unto the LORD thy God, thou shalt not slack to pay it, for he will surely require it of thee.
Numbers 30:2: If a man vow a vow unto the LORD or swear an oath to bind his soul, he shall not break his word but do all that proceedeth out of his mouth.
Psalm 76:11: Vow and pay unto the LORD your God, let all that be round about him bring presents unto him that ought to be feared.
Hebrews 9:27: It is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment.

translationNotes.term: Take back his words before the time
translationNotes.note: A vow was a binding public promise, usually to give something once a request had been answered. Numbers 30:2 says a man shall not break his word, and Ecclesiastes 5:4-5 says it is better not to vow at all than to vow and fail to pay.

The window for changing course closes at death in this book's account. Hebrews 9:27 sets out the same sequence, appointed once to die and after that the judgment, and this chapter ties it specifically to promises left unpaid.

The phrase turns up twice in this short chapter with opposite senses, first of a man withdrawing his word early and then of work done ahead of its proper moment. In both cases the fault named is acting outside the appointed time rather than the act itself.

Emunah means steadiness and reliability before it means belief, and Exodus 17:12 uses it of Moses' hands being steady until the going down of the sun. Bringing gifts with faith means bringing them dependably, which is why patience stands in the same sentence.

translationNotes.term: Deceit before men, and sin before God
translationNotes.note: The chapter separates the two audiences deliberately. What men see is a fraud and what God sees is sin, so one act is charged twice on different counts. That pairing runs through the whole second half of the book wherever public conduct is judged.

stories.keyTakeaway: Enoch says a gift brought patiently and in faith brings forgiveness, but a man who takes back what he promised, or lets the time run out without doing it, has no repentance left to him once he is dead.

stories.title: 📜 2 Enoch (Secrets of Enoch) 63
summaryBullets: When man clothes the naked and fills the hungry, he will find reward from God. (63:1).
But if his heart murmur, he commits a double evil; ruin of himself and of that which he gives; and for him there will be no finding of reward on account of that. (63:2).

And if his own heart is filled with his food and his own flesh, clothed with his own clothing, he commits contempt, and will forfeit all his endurance of poverty, and will not find reward of his good deeds. (63:3).

Every proud and magniloquent man is hateful to the Lord, and every false speech, clothed in untruth; it will be cut with the blade of the sword of death, and thrown into the fire, and shall burn for all time. (63:4).
crossRefs: Isaiah 58:7: Deal thy bread to the hungry, bring the poor that are cast out to thy house, and when thou seest the naked, cover him.
Proverbs 16:5: Every one that is proud in heart is an abomination to the LORD, and though hand join in hand he shall not be unpunished.
James 4:16: Ye rejoice in your boastings, and all such rejoicing is evil.
1 Peter 4:9: Use hospitality one to another without grudging.
Matthew 6:1-4: Take heed that ye do not your alms before men to be seen of them, but let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth.

translationNotes.note: The grumbling is charged as two offences at once, damage to the giver and damage to the gift, so an act that would have counted is cancelled out. 1 Peter 4:9 states the same rule in a single line, use hospitality one to another without grudging.

Speaking big. The word is built from the Latin for great and for speak, and it names a boaster rather than a liar. James 4:16 says all such rejoicing in boasting is evil, and Proverbs 16:5 calls the proud in heart an abomination to the LORD.

The phrase treats what a man has already put up with as something he can still lose. A giver who fills himself from his own food and clothes himself from his own cloth while giving forfeits the credit of every hardship he has borne, which is how the chapter reckons it.

Speech is described as a garment with something else underneath. Proverbs 26:23 uses the same picture for burning lips over a wicked heart, a potsherd covered with silver dross, and this chapter then has the covering cut through.

translationNotes.term: The blade of the sword of death
translationNotes.note: Cut, thrown into the fire and burning are three stages of one sentence, and the sequence is how a felled tree was dealt with. Matthew 3:10 uses the same order, the axe laid to the root, the tree hewn down, and the wood cast into the fire.

stories.keyTakeaway: Clothing the naked and feeding the hungry earns a reward, but grumbling over it wrecks both the giver and the gift. Enoch closes on the proud and boastful man and on false speech, which is cut down, thrown into the fire and burned.

stories.title: 📜 2 Enoch (Secrets of Enoch) 64
summaryBullets: When Enoch had spoken these words to his sons, all people far and near heard how the Lord was calling Enoch. They took counsel together: (64:1).
Let us go and kiss Enoch, and two thousand men came together and came to the place Achuzan where Enoch was, and his sons. (64:2).
And the elders of the people, the whole assembly, came and bowed down and began to kiss Enoch and said to him: (64:3).
Our father Enoch, (may) you (be) blessed of the Lord, the eternal ruler, and now bless your sons and all the people, that we may be glorified to-day before your face. (64:4).

For you shalt be glorified before the Lord's face for all time, since the Lord chose you, rather than all men on earth, and designated you writer of all his creation, visible (physical) and invisible (spiritual), and redeemed of the sins of man, and helper of your household. (64:5).
crossRefs: Genesis 47:7-10: Jacob is brought in before Pharaoh and blesses him, so a blessing given by an elder to a ruler was a recognised public act.
Genesis 48:9-16: Joseph brings his sons near, and Jacob kisses them and embraces them before he lays his hands on them and blesses them.
Deuteronomy 34:8: The children of Israel wept for Moses in the plains of Moab thirty days, so a whole people gathering at a leader's departure is the expected thing.
Acts 20:36-38: They all wept sore, fell on Paul's neck and kissed him, sorrowing most of all that they should see his face no more.
1 Enoch 12:3-4: The Watchers call Enoch the scribe of righteousness, the same office the assembly names for him here.

translationNotes.note: The Hebrew word achuzzah means a holding or possession, land held by right, and Genesis 17:8 uses it of Canaan given for an everlasting possession. This book names Achuzan as the place where Enoch was taken up and where the altar is later built, and says nothing at all about where it lies.

A kiss was a formal greeting between kinsmen and a mark of respect to a superior, not a private gesture. Genesis 48:10 has Jacob kiss his grandsons before blessing them, and Acts 20:37 has a whole company kiss Paul as he leaves for the last time.

The book counts the crowd. Numbers all through this text are exact, whether it is two hundred angels over the stars or three hundred and sixty-six books, and the assembly at the end gets the same treatment.

Qahal means the whole body of people called together, and the Greek Septuagint renders it ekklesia, the word the New Testament uses for a church. Here it means the gathered population and nothing institutional.

translationNotes.term: Redeemed of the sins of man
translationNotes.note: These are the words the assembly speaks to Enoch, set beside their calling him writer of all creation and helper of his household. The book is reporting what the crowd said to his face on the day he left.

stories.keyTakeaway: Word gets round that the Lord is calling Enoch, and two thousand men come to the place Achuzan to kiss him. The elders and the whole assembly bow down and ask him to bless them, calling him the writer of all creation.

stories.title: 📜 2 Enoch (Secrets of Enoch) 65
summaryBullets: And Enoch answered all his people saying: Hear, my children, before that all creatures were created, the Lord created the visible (physical) and invisible (spiritual) things. (65:1).

And as much time as there was and went past, understand that after all that he created man in the likeness of his own form, and put into him eyes to see, and ears to hear, and heart to reflect, and intellect with which to deliberate. (65:2).

And the Lord saw all man's works, and created all his creatures, and divided time, from time he fixed the years, and from the years he appointed the months, and from the months he appointed the days, and of days he appointed seven. (65:3).

And in those he appointed the hours, measured them out exactly, that man might reflect on time and count years, months, and hours, (their) alternation, beginning, and end, and that he might count his own life, from the beginning until death, and reflect on his sin and write his work bad and good; because no work is hidden before the Lord, that every man might know his works and never transgress all his commandments, and keep my handwriting from generation to generation. (65:4).

When all creation visible (physical) and invisible (spiritual), as the Lord created it, shall end, then every man goes to the great judgment, and then all time shall perish, and the years, and thenceforward there will be neither months nor days nor hours, they will be adhered together and will not be counted. (65:5).

There will be one aeon, and all the righteous who shall escape the Lord's great judgment, shall be collected in the great aeon, for the righteous the great aeon will begin, and they will live eternally, and then too there will be amongst them neither labour, nor sickness, nor humiliation, nor anxiety, nor need, nor brutality, nor night, nor darkness, but great light. (65:6).
And they shall have a great indestructible wall, and a paradise bright and incorruptible (eternal), for all corruptible (mortal) things shall pass away, and there will be eternal life. (65:7).
crossRefs: Genesis 1:14: Let them be for signs and for seasons and for days and years, the division of time this chapter is describing.
Psalm 90:12: So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.
Revelation 21:4: God shall wipe away all tears, and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow nor crying, neither any more pain.
Revelation 21:23-25: The city has no need of the sun or the moon, there is no night there, and the gates are not shut at all by day.
Isaiah 65:17-19: Behold, I create new heavens and a new earth, and the voice of weeping shall be no more heard in her.

translationNotes.note: Aion means an age, a stretch of time with a start and a finish. Saying there will be one aeon after the judgment means the divisions stop and a single unbroken age is left, which is why the chapter lists years, months, days and hours as things that perish with the rest.

The week is the one unit of time not tied to anything in the sky. A year is solar, a month lunar, a day one turn of the earth, but a seven-day cycle answers to nothing overhead. Genesis 2:2-3 grounds it in the days of creation, and this chapter lists it as a deliberate cut in time.

A wall is what makes a city safe, and a broken one was the standing picture of ruin, as at Nehemiah 1:3, where the wall of Jerusalem is broken down and the gates burned. Revelation 21:12 gives the new Jerusalem a wall great and high.

In Hebrew the heart is where a man thinks and decides rather than where he feels; Proverbs 23:7 says as he thinketh in his heart, so is he. This chapter lists it beside the eyes and the ears as an organ with a job, which is exactly how the vocabulary works.

Not subject to decay. The same word stood at the third heaven earlier in this book, for the border that paradise sits on, and here it describes the final paradise itself, so the book ends by putting the righteous on the far side of a line it drew at the start of the journey.

The reason given for dividing time at all is so that a man can measure his own life against it and keep his own record. Psalm 90:12 asks for exactly that, to be taught to number our days so as to apply the heart unto wisdom.

stories.keyTakeaway: Enoch traces time itself: God cut it into years, months, days, sevens and hours so that a man could count his own life. At the judgment time stops, and the righteous are gathered into one age with no night, no sickness and no end.

stories.title: 📜 2 Enoch (Secrets of Enoch) 66
summaryBullets: And now, my children, keep your souls from all injustice, such as the Lord hates. (66:1).
Walk before his face with terror and trembling and serve him alone. (66:2).
Bow down to the true God, not to dumb idols, but bow down to his similitude, and bring all just offerings before the Lord's face. The Lord hates what is unjust. (66:3).

For the Lord sees all things; when man takes thought in his heart, then he counsels the intellects, and every thought is always before the Lord, who made firm the earth and put all creatures on it. (66:4).
If you look to heaven, the Lord is there; if you take thought of the sea's deep and all the under-earth, the Lord is there. (66:5).
For the Lord created all things. Bow not down to things made by man, leaving the Lord of all creation, because no work can remain hidden before the Lord's face. (66:6).

Walk, my children, in long-suffering, in meekness, honesty, in provocation, in grief, in faith and in truth, in (reliance on) promises, in illness, in abuse, in wounds, in temptation, in nakedness, in privation, loving one another, till you go out from this age of ills, that you become inheritors of endless time. (66:7).

Blessed are the just who shall escape the great judgment, for they shall shine forth more than the sun sevenfold, for in this world the seventh part is taken off from all, light, darkness, food, enjoyment, sorrow, paradise, torture, fire, frost, and other things; he put all down in writing, that you might read and understand. (66:8).
crossRefs: Psalm 139:7-10: Whither shall I go from thy spirit? If I ascend up into heaven thou art there, if I make my bed in hell, behold, thou art there.
Exodus 20:4-5: Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, nor bow down to them nor serve them.
Isaiah 44:9-17: A man fells a tree, burns half of it to warm himself and bake his bread, and makes the rest into a god and falls down before it.
Matthew 13:43: Then shall the righteous shine forth as the sun in the kingdom of their Father.
Daniel 12:3: They that be wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament, and they that turn many to righteousness as the stars for ever and ever.

translationNotes.note: The Hebrew word for idols sounds like the word for nothing and works as an insult, meaning worthless things. Isaiah 44:9-17 walks through the process in detail, a man felling a tree, burning half of it to bake his bread, and bowing down to the piece that is left over.

translationNotes.term: Shine forth more than the sun sevenfold
translationNotes.note: Sevenfold is the standard multiplier for full measure in this vocabulary. Isaiah 30:26 says the light of the sun shall be sevenfold, as the light of seven days, and Matthew 13:43 has the righteous shine forth as the sun.

translationNotes.term: The seventh part is taken off from all
translationNotes.note: This is the book's explanation for why the present world is dimmer than the one coming: everything here, light and darkness, food and sorrow alike, runs at six parts out of seven. It is stated as a fact of the current order and not argued for.

translationNotes.original: Greek: φόβος καὶ τρόμος (phobos kai tromos)
translationNotes.note: The pair is a set phrase for how a subordinate comes before a superior. Philippians 2:12 uses it of working out salvation with fear and trembling, and Psalm 2:11 says serve the LORD with fear and rejoice with trembling.

translationNotes.term: In provocation, in grief, in nakedness, in privation
translationNotes.note: A hardship list of the kind used to describe a working life under pressure. 2 Corinthians 11:23-27 runs a longer one of the same sort, and 2 Corinthians 6:4-10 pairs each hardship with what holds through it, which is the shape this sentence takes.

The line forbids handmade images and then tells them to bow to his likeness. This book said earlier that man was made in the likeness of God's own face, and that reviling a man's face is reviling God's, so the two halves of the sentence are held together by that.

stories.keyTakeaway: Enoch's last instruction: serve God alone, bow to nothing made by hand, and know that no thought is hidden and no place is out of reach. He tells them to walk in long-suffering through every hardship, and says the just will shine sevenfold.

stories.title: 📜 2 Enoch (Secrets of Enoch) 67
summaryBullets: When Enoch had talked to the people, the Lord sent out darkness on to the earth, and there was darkness, and it covered those men standing with Enoch, and they took Enoch up on to the highest heaven, where the Lord (is); and he received him and placed him before his face, and the darkness went off from the earth, and light came again. (67:1).
And the people saw and understood not how Enoch had been taken, and glorified God, and found a roll in which was traced The Invisible (spiritual) God; and all went to their dwelling places. (67:2).
crossRefs: Genesis 5:24: Enoch walked with God and was not, for God took him.
2 Kings 2:11: A chariot of fire and horses of fire part the two men, and Elijah goes up by a whirlwind into heaven.
Acts 1:9: While they beheld, he was taken up, and a cloud received him out of their sight.
Exodus 20:21: The people stood afar off and Moses drew near unto the thick darkness where God was.
Exodus 10:21-23: A thick darkness comes over Egypt for three days so that no man rose from his place, while the children of Israel had light.

translationNotes.note: The darkness works as a screen so that nobody sees the removal happen. Exodus 20:21 puts God in the thick darkness on Sinai and Exodus 10:21-23 uses darkness as a plague that stops all movement, so darkness in this vocabulary covers as readily as it punishes.

A megillah is a scroll, sheets glued end to end and wound on a rod, which is what a book was. Jeremiah 36:2 has one written to hold everything the prophet had spoken, and Ezekiel 2:9-10 has one held out already written on both sides.

Invisible, not able to be seen. Colossians 1:15 calls him the image of the invisible God and 1 Timothy 1:17 speaks of the King eternal, immortal, invisible. This book has used the visible and invisible pair since its creation account, and it closes the removal with that same word.

translationNotes.term: Understood not how Enoch had been taken
translationNotes.note: The witnesses see the result and never the mechanism, which is where Genesis 5:24 also leaves the reader. This book supplies a crowd, a darkness and a date, and still lets nobody watch the moment itself.

The phrase repeats what was said at the throne earlier in the book, that Enoch should stand before God's face into eternity. The removal scene closes the loop the ascent opened, using the same words in both places.

stories.keyTakeaway: Darkness comes down over the crowd, and when it lifts Enoch is gone, taken to the highest heaven and set before the Lord's face. The people cannot work out how it happened, glorify God, and find a roll inscribed The Invisible God.

stories.title: 📜 2 Enoch (Secrets of Enoch) 68
summaryBullets: Enoch was born on the sixth day of the month Tsivan, and lived three hundred and sixty-five years. (68:1).
He was taken up to heaven on the first day of the month Tsivan and remained in heaven sixty days. (68:2).

He wrote all these signs of all creation, which the Lord created, and wrote three hundred and sixty-six books, and handed them over to his sons and remained on earth thirty days, and was again taken up to heaven on the sixth day of the month Tsivan, on the very day and hour when he was born. (68:3).
As every man's nature in this life is dark, so are also his conception, birth, and departure from this life. (68:4).
At what hour he was conceived, at that hour he was born, and at that hour too he died. (68:5).
Methosalam (Methuselah) and his brethren, all the sons of Enoch, made haste, and erected an altar at that place called Achuzan, from where and where Enoch had been taken up to heaven. (68:6).
And they took sacrificial oxen and summoned all people and sacrificed the sacrifice before the Lord's face. (68:7).
All people, the elders of the people and the whole assembly came to the feast and brought gifts to the sons of Enoch. (68:8).

And they made a great feast, rejoicing and making merry three days, praising God, who had given them such a sign through Enoch, who had found favour with him, and that they should hand it on to their sons from generation to generation, from age to age. (68:9).
crossRefs: Genesis 5:23-24: All the days of Enoch were three hundred sixty and five years, and he walked with God and was not, for God took him.
Genesis 8:20: Noah builds an altar to the LORD and offers burnt offerings of every clean beast and every clean fowl.
Genesis 12:7-8: Abram builds an altar to the LORD who appeared to him, and another between Bethel and Hai, and calls on the name of the LORD.
Exodus 24:4-5: Moses builds an altar under the hill with twelve pillars, and young men offer burnt offerings and sacrifice peace offerings of oxen.
Deuteronomy 16:13-15: The feast is kept for seven days with the whole household, the servant, the stranger, the fatherless and the widow rejoicing together.

translationNotes.note: The narrative stops here, with the altar, the feast and Amen. Longer Slavonic manuscripts run on past this point, with the priesthood passing to Methuselah and then to Nir and with the birth of Melchizedek. That section is not in the manuscript behind this English text, so a reader who came looking for the Melchizedek material will not find it here. Scripture's own account of Melchizedek stands at Genesis 14:18-20.

The third month, falling across May and June, and named at Esther 8:9. Every date in this chapter sits inside that one month: born on the sixth, taken up on the first, and taken finally on the sixth again.

Both spans are stated flatly, sixty days above and thirty back on earth teaching. The thirty match the term God set when he sent Enoch down, so the closing chapter is squaring its own account. The final removal is dated to the day of his birth, which is the point the chapter is making.

The same place where the crowd had gathered. An altar goes up there because that is where Enoch went up, which follows the ordinary pattern of building where something happened, as Genesis 12:7 has Abram build where the LORD appeared to him. The book never says where Achuzan is.

An ox was the most expensive animal a man could bring, which is why it turns up at the largest occasions. Exodus 24:5 has oxen offered when the covenant is sealed at Sinai, and Genesis 8:20 has Noah offer of every clean beast after the flood.

A sacrifice was followed by eating the meat together, so the feast is the second half of the offering and not a party bolted onto it. Deuteronomy 16:13-15 sets out that pattern, with the household, the servants, the stranger, the fatherless and the widow all eating together.

Amen comes from a root meaning firm or reliable, and it is the word a hearer says to make a statement his own. Deuteronomy 27:15-26 has the people answer Amen to every curse read out, and 1 Chronicles 16:36 has all the people say Amen and praise the LORD. Here it closes the book.

stories.keyTakeaway: The book closes with dates. Enoch was born on the sixth of Tsivan, lived three hundred and sixty-five years, spent sixty days in heaven and thirty back on earth, and was taken on the day and hour of his birth. His sons build an altar at Achuzan and keep a three-day feast.

intro:
2 Enoch is transmitted under the name of Enoch son of Jared, the same figure Genesis 5:21-24 records as having walked with God before God took him. It is also called Slavonic Enoch, from the language of every manuscript known before 2009, and the Book of the Secrets of Enoch, from the title its Slavonic copies carry. The numeral is a modern convention distinguishing it from the Ge'ez 1 Enoch and the Hebrew 3 Enoch, and there is no literary dependence in either direction: 2 Enoch shares Enoch's name and his ascent, and almost nothing else, with the Ge'ez book.

The narrative opens in the last days of Enoch's life on earth. Two men of immense appearance stand at his bed and carry him up on the wings of the wind (1:1-2:3), and he is taken through ten heavens in order: the storehouses of snow, rain, and dew and the two hundred angels who govern the stars (3-6); the imprisoned angels awaiting judgment in the second (7); paradise with the tree of life, and the place of torment, in the third (8-10); the courses of the sun and the moon in the fourth, with their gates counted and measured (11-16); the armed hosts who sing before the Lord (17), the mourning watchers of the fifth heaven (18), and the archangels of the sixth, who keep the orders of the stars and the seasons (19); and the throne of glory in the tenth, where Michael and Gabriel bring him and where he falls on his face (20-22). The Lord orders the archangel Pravuil to bring out the books, and Enoch writes for thirty days and thirty nights and produces three hundred and sixty-six books (23:1-6). God then dictates to him an account of creation that stands outside Genesis, out of the invisible into the visible, day by day, with the planets set on their circles under their Greek names (24-33). Enoch is returned to earth for thirty days to instruct his sons (36-38), and the second half of the book is that instruction: charity to the naked and the hungry, offerings brought with faith, justice for the orphan and the widow, restraint of the tongue, and warnings against idolatry and revenge (39-66). The Lord sends darkness over the earth and Enoch is taken for the last time (67:1-2). The closing chapter dates his birth and his removal to the sixth day of the month Tsivan and gives his life as three hundred and sixty-five years (68:1-3). This text ends there. The longer Slavonic recension continues to chapter 73 with the priesthood passing from Methuselah to Nir and the birth of Melchizedek from the body of Nir's dead wife; that section is absent here, as it was from the 1896 English translation of W. R. Morfill, edited by R. H. Charles, which ended at chapter 68.

The calendar material is worth reading closely because the book counts in two ways. The sun is given one hundred and eighty-two thrones for the shortening days and one hundred and eighty-two for the lengthening, which is a year of three hundred and sixty-four days (48:1), while the account of the solar gates fixes the year at three hundred and sixty-five days and a quarter and the lunar year at three hundred and fifty-four (14:1; 16:3), and sets the great cycle at five hundred and thirty-two years (16:4).

The manuscripts are Slavonic and late. The longer recension is carried by R and J, both sixteenth century, and P, dated 1679; the shorter by U, fifteenth century, and B, V, and N, sixteenth and seventeenth. A. Popov published the first complete edition in 1880, and Matvei Sokolov's edition, finished by M. N. Speranskij, appeared in 1910. In 1972 the Egypt Exploration Society excavated four Coptic parchment fragments at Qasr Ibrim in Christian Nubia; Joost Hagen identified them as 2 Enoch and announced the identification at the Fifth Enoch Seminar in Naples in June 2009, matching them to chapters 36 to 42. The identification has been contested and defended in print since. The date is genuinely open and the proposals are far apart. (1) R. H. Charles, in the 1896 edition, placed it in the first century AD before the destruction of the temple, since the book speaks of sacrifice and offering as things still being brought (59:1-3; 61:3-4; 62:1). (2) Andre Vaillant argued that the work is Christian in origin, and J. T. Milik, in 1976, dated it to the ninth or tenth century AD and to a Greek monk, arguing from vocabulary he found no earlier than the ninth century. (3) Christfried Bottrich and Andrei Orlov have argued for a Jewish work of the first century AD. The Coptic fragments, if they belong to this book, put a copy of it in Nubia several centuries before any Slavonic copy was made. No communion receives 2 Enoch as canonical.
